claims.source: The striatum is primarily composed of GABAergic striatal projection neurons (SPNs), which make up two functionally distinct output pathways: the D1-receptor expressing cells of the direct pathway (dSPNs), which project to substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr), and the D2-receptor expressing cells of the indirect pathway (iSPNs), which project to external globus pallidus (GPe; Calabresi et al., 2014; Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011; Kravitz et al., 2010; Tai et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: dSPNs express D1-receptors and project to substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr).
claims.source: The striatum is primarily composed of GABAergic striatal projection neurons (SPNs), which make up two functionally distinct output pathways: the D1-receptor expressing cells of the direct pathway (dSPNs), which project to substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr), and the D2-receptor expressing cells of the indirect pathway (iSPNs), which project to external globus pallidus (GPe; Calabresi et al., 2014; Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011; Kravitz et al., 2010; Tai et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: iSPNs express D2-receptors and project to external globus pallidus (GPe).
claims.source: The striatum is primarily composed of GABAergic striatal projection neurons (SPNs), which make up two functionally distinct output pathways: the D1-receptor expressing cells of the direct pathway (dSPNs), which project to substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr), and the D2-receptor expressing cells of the indirect pathway (iSPNs), which project to external globus pallidus (GPe; Calabresi et al., 2014; Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011; Kravitz et al., 2010; Tai et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: SPNs receive excitatory glutamatergic inputs from cortex and thalamus, as well as dopaminergic input from the midbrain.
claims.source: The two types of SPNs are intermixed throughout the striatum and receive excitatory glutamatergic inputs from cortex and thalamus, as well as dopaminergic input from the midbrain (Ding et al., 2008; Doig et al., 2010; Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Coordinated activity between the populations of SPNs mediates action selection, motor learning, and habit formation.
claims.source: Coordinated activity between the populations of SPNs in response to these inputs mediates action selection, motor learning, and habit formation (Hawes et al., 2015; Santos et al., 2015; Yin et al., 2005; Yin et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: SPNs comprise upwards of 95% of the cells in the striatum.
claims.source: Although SPNs comprise upwards of 95% of the cells in the striatum, there are distinct types of GABAergic interneurons that contribute significantly to the inhibitory circuitry of the striatum.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about striatal composition.

claims.claim: Parvalbumin (PV) interneurons make up ~2% of the cells in the striatum.
claims.source: Parvalbumin (PV) interneurons, which make up ~2% of the cells in the striatum, provide the largest feedforward inhibition onto SPNs (Burke et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Burke et al., 2017.

claims.claim: PV interneurons provide the largest feedforward inhibition onto SPNs.
claims.source: Parvalbumin (PV) interneurons, which make up ~2% of the cells in the striatum, provide the largest feedforward inhibition onto SPNs (Burke et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Burke et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Changes in the number and/or function of PV interneurons have been identified in several ASD mouse models, including Cntnap2-/- mice.
claims.source: Changes in the number and/or function of PV interneurons have been identified in several ASD mouse models, including Cntnap2-/- mice, implicating PV circuitry as a potential common alteration across ASD mouse models (Filice et al., 2020; Juarez and Martínez Cerdeño, 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Filice et al., 2020; Juarez and Martínez Cerdeño, 2022.

claims.claim: dSPNs in Cntnap2-/- mice exhibited increased spike probability compared to wild-type (WT) dSPNs.
claims.source: We quantified the number of evoked APs at different light intensities and found that dSPNs in young adult Cntnap2-/- mice exhibited increased spike probability compared to wild-type (WT) dSPNs (Figure 1B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claims.claim: The interaction effect of genotype and stimulation intensity in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs suggests increased corticostriatal drive.
claims.source: The interaction effect of genotype and stimulation intensity in these cells suggests increased corticostriatal drive, consistent with findings in another mouse model with loss of function of the ASD-risk gene Tsc1 (Benthall et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the data, supported by comparison to another study.

claims.claim: Cntnap2-/- iSPNs had subtly increased cortically-evoked AP firing compared to WT iSPNs, although this was not statistically significant.
claims.source: Cntnap2-/- iSPNs had subtly increased cortically-evoked AP firing compared to WT iSPNs, although this was not statistically significant (Figure 1D and E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claims.claim: The average optically evoked EPSC amplitude was not significantly different across a range of light intensities in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs or iSPNs compared to WT.
claims.source: We found that the average optically evoked EPSC amplitude was not significantly different across a range of light intensities in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs or iSPNs compared to WT (Figure 1F–I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F-I.

claims.claim: There were no significant differences in AMPA:NMDA ratio in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs or iSPNs.
claims.source: In an additional group of mice, we measured the ratio of AMPAR currents recorded at −70 mV to NMDAR currents recorded at +40 mV (at 20% blue light intensity) and found no significant differences in AMPA:NMDA ratio in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs or iSPNs (Figure 1J–M).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J-M.

claims.claim: Cntnap2-/- SPNs in adult mice had similar spine density as WT.
claims.source: We found that Cntnap2-/- SPNs in adult mice had similar spine density as WT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting no overall change in synapse number.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The enhanced cortically driven spiking in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs is not due to a change in corticostriatal synaptic strength or overall synapse density.
claims.source: Together, these results show that dSPNs in Cntnap2-/- mice exhibit enhanced cortically driven spiking. However, this is not due to a change in corticostriatal synaptic strength or overall synapse density.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Previous work has indicated a reduction in the number and/or function of fast-spiking parvalbumin-expressing (PV) interneurons across multiple brain regions in Cntnap2-/- mice.
claims.source: Previous work has indicated a reduction in the number and/or function of fast-spiking parvalbumin-expressing (PV) interneurons across multiple brain regions in Cntnap2-/- mice (Ahmed et al., 2023; Antoine et al., 2019; Jurgensen and Castillo, 2015; Paterno et al., 2021; Peñagarikano et al., 2011; Vogt et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: Deficits in inhibition have been identified in the cortex and hippocampus of Cntnap2-/- mice.
claims.source: While deficits in inhibition have been identified in the cortex and hippocampus (Antoine et al., 2019; Jurgensen and Castillo, 2015), and the number of PV interneurons has been reported to be decreased in the striatum (Peñagarikano et al., 2011), a comprehensive assessment of striatal inhibitory synaptic function has yet to be completed in Cntnap2-/- mice.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Antoine et al., 2019; Jurgensen and Castillo, 2015.

claims.claim: The number of PV interneurons has been reported to be decreased in the striatum of Cntnap2-/- mice.
claims.source: While deficits in inhibition have been identified in the cortex and hippocampus (Antoine et al., 2019; Jurgensen and Castillo, 2015), and the number of PV interneurons has been reported to be decreased in the striatum (Peñagarikano et al., 2011), a comprehensive assessment of striatal inhibitory synaptic function has yet to be completed in Cntnap2-/- mice.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Peñagarikano et al., 2011.

claims.claim: In Cntnap2-/- dSPNs and iSPNs, the average amplitude of electrically evoked IPSCs across a range of stimulation intensities was not different from WT.
claims.source: In Cntnap2-/- dSPNs and iSPNs, the average amplitude of electrically evoked IPSCs across a range of stimulation intensities was not different from WT (Figure 2B–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-E.

claims.claim: The average amplitude of optically-evoked IPSCs did not differ significantly in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs or iSPNs compared to WT controls.
claims.source: We found that the average amplitude of optically-evoked IPSCs did not differ significantly in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs or iSPNs compared to WT controls (Figure 2G–J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-J.

claims.claim: There were no significant differences in the intrinsic excitability of PV interneurons in Cntnap2-/- mice compared to controls.
claims.source: Plotting the number of APs fired as a function of current step amplitude indicated that there were no significant differences in the intrinsic excitability of PV interneurons in Cntnap2-/- mice compared to controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claims.claim: There were no changes in intrinsic cell properties such as rheobase, membrane resistance, capacitance, resting membrane potential, or AP shape in Cntnap2-/- PV interneurons.
claims.source: There were also no changes in intrinsic cell properties such as rheobase, membrane resistance, capacitance, resting membrane potential, or AP shape in Cntnap2-/- PV interneurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-K.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in the number of PV-positive cells in the dorsal striatum of Cntnap2-/- mice compared to WT.
claims.source: We found no significant difference in the number of PV-positive cells in the dorsal striatum of Cntnap2-/- mice compared to WT (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–F and K–N).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-F and K-N.

claims.claim: There were no changes in the average single cell or total level of PV protein expression in the dorsal striatum of Cntnap2-/- mice.
claims.source: We also found no changes in the average single cell or total level of PV protein expression in the dorsal striatum (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G–J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G-J.

claims.claim: There were no significant changes in PV interneuron number, PV expression, or PV interneuron-mediated inhibition in the adult Cntnap2-/- striatum compared to WT controls.
claims.source: Overall, we did not observe significant changes in PV interneuron number, PV expression, or PV interneuron-mediated inhibition in the adult Cntnap2-/- striatum compared to WT controls.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Cntnap2-/- dSPNs had significantly increased intrinsic excitability compared to WT dSPNs.
claims.source: We found that Cntnap2-/- dSPNs had significantly increased intrinsic excitability compared to WT dSPNs (Figure 3A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claims.claim: Cntnap2-/- dSPNs had reduced rheobase current.
claims.source: Cntnap2-/- dSPNs also had reduced rheobase current (Figure 3C), the minimum current required to evoke an AP, as well as increased membrane resistance (Figure 3D).

claims.claim: Cntnap2-/- dSPNs had increased membrane resistance.
claims.source: Cntnap2-/- dSPNs also had reduced rheobase current (Figure 3C), the minimum current required to evoke an AP, as well as increased membrane resistance (Figure 3D).

claims.claim: There was a trend towards increased excitability in Cntnap2-/- iSPNs, but this effect was not statistically significant.

claims.claim: Cntnap2-/- iSPNs did not exhibit changes in rheobase current or membrane resistance.
claims.source: While there was a trend towards increased excitability in Cntnap2-/- iSPNs, this effect was not statistically significant (Figure 3G–H), and these cells did not exhibit changes in rheobase current (Figure 3I) or membrane resistance (Figure 3J).

claims.claim: Membrane capacitance, resting membrane potential, and AP shape were not significantly changed in Cntnap2-/- SPNs.
claims.source: Membrane capacitance (Figure 3E and K), resting membrane potential (Figure 3F and L), and AP shape (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) were not significantly changed in Cntnap2-/- SPNs, although latency to first spike was reduced in both Cntnap2-/- dSPNs and iSPNs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E, K, F, L, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Latency to first spike was reduced in both Cntnap2-/- dSPNs and iSPNs.
claims.source: Membrane capacitance (Figure 3E and K), resting membrane potential (Figure 3F and L), and AP shape (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) were not significantly changed in Cntnap2-/- SPNs, although latency to first spike was reduced in both Cntnap2-/- dSPNs and iSPNs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and I.

claims.claim: The increase in dSPN intrinsic excitability likely underlies the enhanced corticostriatal drive in Cntnap2-/- mice.
claims.source: Given the lack of synaptic changes observed in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs, the increase in dSPN intrinsic excitability likely underlies their enhanced corticostriatal drive (see Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Caspr2 is known to be involved in the clustering of voltage-gated potassium channels, particularly Kv1.2 channels.
claims.source: Caspr2 is known to be involved in the clustering of voltage-gated potassium channels (Inda et al., 2006; Poliak et al., 1999; Poliak et al., 2003), particularly Kv1.2 channels (Scott et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: Kv1.2 channels play an important role in regulating the intrinsic excitability of SPNs.
claims.source: These channels play an important role in regulating the intrinsic excitability of SPNs (Nisenbaum et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nisenbaum et al., 1994.

claims.claim: Blockade of Kv1.2 channels with α-Dendrotoxin (α-DTX) results in increased AP frequency, decreased rheobase current, decreased first AP latency, and decreased AP threshold, particularly in dSPNs.
claims.source: Blockade of these channels with the drug α-Dendrotoxin (α-DTX) results in increased AP frequency, decreased rheobase current, decreased first AP latency, and decreased AP threshold (Shen et al., 2004), particularly in dSPNs (Lahiri and Bevan, 2020).

claims.claim: α-DTX enhanced AP firing and decreased AP threshold in WT dSPNs, but not in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs.

claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-F.

claims.claim: AP width was significantly increased by α-DTX in WT but not Cntnap2-/- dSPNs.
claims.source: AP width was also significantly increased by α-DTX in WT but not Cntnap2-/- dSPNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and Q), while AP fast afterhyperpolarization and AP latency were significantly decreased in both WT and Cntnap2-/- dSPNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, I, N and R).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and Q.

claims.claim: AP fast afterhyperpolarization and AP latency were significantly decreased by α-DTX in both WT and Cntnap2-/- dSPNs.
claims.source: AP width was also significantly increased by α-DTX in WT but not Cntnap2-/- dSPNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and Q), while AP fast afterhyperpolarization and AP latency were significantly decreased in both WT and Cntnap2-/- dSPNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, I, N and R).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, I, N and R.

claims.claim: The effects of α-DTX on Cntnap2-/- dSPNs are largely occluded, indicating that Kv1.2 channels are basally altered by loss of Cntnap2.
claims.source: Together, these data show that the effects of α-DTX on Cntnap2-/- dSPNs are largely occluded, indicating that Kv1.2 channels are basally altered by loss of Cntnap2.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Altered Kv1.2 channels likely account for the enhanced intrinsic excitability of Cntnap2-/- dSPNs.
claims.source: This likely accounts for the enhanced intrinsic excitability of Cntnap2-/- dSPNs.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claims.claim: α-DTX had minimal effects on WT and Cntnap2-/- iSPNs.
claims.source: We tested the effects of α-DTX on WT and Cntnap2-/- iSPNs and found minimal changes (Figure 4G–K, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), with no alterations in AP threshold (Figure 4I and L) and only a small shift in the input-output relationship of Cntnap2-/- iSPNs (Figure 4K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G-K and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: There is a difference in the sensitivity of dSPNs and iSPNs to Kv1 blockade.
claims.source: The effects of α-DTX on iSPN excitability have been less well documented, and our data suggest a difference in the sensitivity of dSPNs and iSPNs to Kv1 blockade.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Alterations in striatal circuits are thought to be involved in the manifestation of RRBs.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in the total distance traveled, average speed, or number of rears in Cntnap2-/- mice compared to WT controls in the open field.
claims.source: In the open field, we found no significant difference in the total distance traveled, average speed, or number of rears in Cntnap2-/- mice compared to WT controls (Figure 5E–G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E-G.

claims.claim: Cntnap2-/- mice made significantly more entries into the center of the open field arena than WT mice.
claims.source: We did find that Cntnap2-/- mice made significantly more entries into the center of the open field arena than WT mice, which may reflect a reduction in avoidance behavior in these mice (Figure 5H).

claims.claim: Cntnap2-/- mice initiated more self-grooming bouts than WT controls in the open field.
claims.source: Manually scored grooming behavior revealed that Cntnap2-/- mice initiated more self-grooming bouts than WT controls in the open field (Figure 5I), consistent with prior reports (Peñagarikano et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I and a citation to Peñagarikano et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Cntnap2-/- mice buried significantly more marbles on average than WT controls.
claims.source: We found that Cntnap2-/- mice buried significantly more marbles on average than WT controls (Figure 5J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J.

claims.claim: Cntnap2-/- mice made significantly more nose pokes within a 10-min period than WT mice in the holeboard assay.

claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5K.

claims.claim: Increased nose poking in Cntnap2-/- mice was largely due to increased poking during the last 5 min of the holeboard test.

claims.claim: Cntnap2-/- mice did not exhibit changes in general locomotor activity compared to WT littermates.

claims.claim: Cntnap2-/- mice had an increase in the total number of grooming bouts.

claims.claim: Decoding models performed significantly better than chance at identifying WT and Cntnap2-/- mice based on their syllable usage and transitions, but not general locomotor activity.

claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5P.

claims.claim: Cntnap2-/- mice performed significantly better than WT mice in the accelerating rotarod task, particularly in the later trials when the rod rotates at the faster 10–80 RPM speed.

claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Cntnap2-/- mice showed no differences during the acquisition phase of the four-choice reversal learning task.
claims.source: During acquisition, Cntnap2-/- mice performed similarly to WT controls, not differing in the average number of trials needed to reach criterion, the number of quadrant entries made before making a choice, or the latency to choose a pot (Figure 7B–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B-D.

claims.claim: Cntnap2-/- mice exhibited typical recall on day 2 of the four-choice reversal learning task.
claims.source: On day 2, Cntnap2-/- mice exhibited typical recall, demonstrating successful consolidation of the odor-reward pairing (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Cntnap2-/- mice had a deficit in reversal learning, requiring significantly more trials on average than WTs to reach criterion once the odor-reward pairing was changed.

claims.claim: Cntnap2-/- mice did not differ from WT controls in choices of the novel or irrelevant odors, or in the number of omitted trials.

claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7K.

claims.claim: The persistence in choosing O1, even after at least one correct choice of O2, drove the cognitive inflexibility in Cntnap2-/- mice.

claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7L.

claims.source: Instead, loss of Cntnap2 resulted in a significant increase in the excitability of dSPNs, likely driven by altered contribution of Kv1.2 channels to intrinsic firing properties.

claims.evidence: This is a general statement supported by the discussion of various studies.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Fernández et al., 2021; Antoine et al., 2019; Cifuentes-Diaz et al., 2023.

results.result: Cntnap2-/- mice exhibit enhanced cortical drive of direct pathway striatal projection neurons (dSPNs), as evidenced by increased spike probability in response to optogenetic cortical stimulation across a range of light intensities.
results.evaluation: Claims C39, C40, and C5 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1B-C showing statistically significant genotype × stimulation interaction (p=0.0321) and main effect of stimulation (p<0.0001). The increased spike probability in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs is consistent and well-documented.

results.result: Cntnap2-/- iSPNs show a subtle, non-significant increase in cortically-evoked action potential firing compared to wild-type iSPNs.
results.evaluation: Claim C41 is supported by data in Figure 1D-E. The authors appropriately report the trend without claiming statistical significance (genotype p=0.3308, interaction p=0.9126), demonstrating rigorous statistical interpretation.

results.result: The enhanced cortical drive in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs is not due to changes in excitatory synaptic strength, AMPA:NMDA ratio, or dendritic spine density.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 are supported by experimental data showing no significant differences in optically evoked EPSC amplitude (Figure 1F-I), AMPA:NMDA ratio (Figure 1J-M), or spine density (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). These negative results appropriately rule out synaptic mechanisms.

results.result: Inhibitory synaptic transmission, PV interneuron function, and PV interneuron number are unchanged in the adult Cntnap2-/- striatum.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C55 are supported by comprehensive experimental data including electrically evoked IPSCs (Figure 2B-E), optically evoked PV-specific IPSCs (Figure 2G-J), PV interneuron intrinsic excitability (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and PV cell counts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). Multiple independent measures converge on the same conclusion.

results.result: Cntnap2-/- dSPNs exhibit significantly increased intrinsic excitability, characterized by increased action potential firing, reduced rheobase current, and increased membrane resistance, which likely underlies the enhanced corticostriatal drive.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 and C63 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3A-D showing statistically significant increases in excitability (genotype × current interaction p=0.0019, genotype p=0.0030), reduced rheobase (p=0.0016), and increased membrane resistance (p=0.0328). The inference linking excitability to cortical drive (C63) is logical given the absence of synaptic changes.

results.result: Cntnap2-/- iSPNs show a non-significant trend toward increased excitability without changes in rheobase current or membrane resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C60 are supported by data in Figure 3G-J. The authors appropriately report the trend without claiming significance (genotype p=0.3130), demonstrating appropriate statistical interpretation and cell-type specificity of the phenotype.

results.result: The effects of Kv1.2 channel blockade with α-DTX are occluded in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs, indicating that Kv1.2 channels are basally altered and likely account for the enhanced intrinsic excitability.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C71 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4A-F showing that α-DTX enhances AP firing and decreases AP threshold in WT but not Cntnap2-/- dSPNs. The occlusion experiment is a strong mechanistic test. However, direct measurement of Kv1.2 channel localization or function would strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: α-DTX has minimal effects on both WT and Cntnap2-/- iSPNs, suggesting differential sensitivity of dSPNs and iSPNs to Kv1 blockade.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 are supported by data in Figure 4G-K and Figure 4—figure supplement 2. The cell-type-specific difference in α-DTX sensitivity is well-documented and helps explain why the Cntnap2 phenotype is more pronounced in dSPNs.

results.result: Cntnap2-/- mice exhibit increased spontaneous repetitive behaviors including self-grooming, marble burying, and nose poking.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C80, C82-C83 are supported by behavioral data showing increased grooming bouts (Figure 5I, p=0.0034), marble burying (Figure 5J, p=0.0396), and nose poking (Figure 5K, p=0.0212). The Keypoint-MoSeq analysis (Figure 5N) provides additional quantitative support for increased grooming.

results.result: Cntnap2-/- mice exhibit reduced entropy in syllable transitions and can be distinguished from WT mice based on syllable usage and transitions but not general locomotor activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 are supported by Keypoint-MoSeq analysis showing reduced entropy (Figure 5O, p=0.0236) and successful decoding based on syllable patterns (Figure 5P). This provides quantitative evidence for behavioral rigidity beyond simple repetition.

results.result: Cntnap2-/- mice show enhanced motor routine learning in the accelerating rotarod task, with increased learning rate but similar initial performance compared to WT mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 are supported by rotarod data showing significant genotype × trial interaction (p<0.0001), no difference in initial performance (Figure 6C, p=0.1518), and increased learning rate (Figure 6D, p=0.0002). The dissociation between initial performance and learning rate is important.

results.result: Cntnap2-/- mice exhibit cognitive inflexibility in reversal learning, requiring more trials to reach criterion due to increased perseverative and regressive errors, despite normal acquisition and recall.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C94 and C96 are supported by four-choice reversal learning data showing normal acquisition (Figure 7B-D) and recall (Figure 7E), but impaired reversal (Figure 7F, p=0.0048) driven by perseverative (p=0.0005) and regressive (p=0.0068) errors (Figure 7K). The behavioral dissociation is well-characterized.

results.result: The authors propose that increased corticostriatal drive may contribute to the acquisition of repetitive, inflexible behaviors in Cntnap2-/- mice, with a connection between DLS physiology and motor routine learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C117, C123, and C124 represent inferences linking physiological and behavioral findings. While the correlation is compelling, the authors acknowledge that causal testing is needed (C117). The lack of direct manipulation experiments (e.g., cell-type-specific rescue) means the mechanistic link remains speculative.

results.result: The authors speculate that divergent cellular changes driven by different ASD risk genes may converge on enhanced corticostriatal drive, potentially contributing to perseverative behaviors across ASD subtypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C126 are explicitly speculative statements about broader implications. While the comparison to other ASD models (e.g., Tsc1, C40, C116) provides some support, this remains a hypothesis requiring testing across multiple models. The speculation is appropriately qualified by the authors.

results.result: Prior literature on PV interneuron alterations in Cntnap2-/- mice is inconsistent across studies and brain regions, with variable reports of cell number and function changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 and C104-C107, C109 accurately summarize the inconsistent prior literature on PV interneurons in Cntnap2-/- mice. The authors appropriately cite multiple studies showing both positive and negative findings, and offer a plausible explanation (C106-C107) for the discrepancies.

results.result: Cntnap2-/- mice show normal general locomotor activity in the open field but increased center entries, suggesting reduced avoidance behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 and C81 are supported by open field data showing no differences in distance traveled, speed, or rears (Figure 5E-G), but increased center entries (Figure 5H, p=0.0101). The interpretation of reduced avoidance is reasonable but could reflect other factors.

results.result: Membrane capacitance, resting membrane potential, and action potential shape are unchanged in Cntnap2-/- SPNs, but latency to first spike is reduced in both dSPNs and iSPNs.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 are supported by data in Figure 3E-F, K-L and Figure 3—figure supplement 1. The reduced latency in both cell types despite differential excitability changes suggests some shared alterations alongside cell-type-specific effects.

results.result: The loss of Caspr2 has variable effects on intrinsic excitability across brain regions and cell types, with increased excitability in dSPNs, Purkinje cells, and some cortical pyramidal cells, potentially due to altered Kv1.2 channel localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C103 synthesize findings from this study and prior literature. The variability across cell types and regions is well-documented through citations (C99-C100). The mechanistic link to Kv1.2 channels (C101-C102) is supported by prior work and the current occlusion experiments, though direct evidence in all cell types is lacking.

results.result: Primary changes in PV interneurons are unlikely to account for altered striatal circuit function in Cntnap2-/- mice.
results.evaluation: Claim C110 is a reasonable inference from the comprehensive negative findings on PV interneuron number, function, and PV-mediated inhibition (C49-C55). However, the authors acknowledge that other interneuron subtypes were not assessed, leaving open the possibility of inhibitory circuit alterations.

results.result: The authors contextualize their findings within established knowledge of striatal subregion function, citing literature on DLS involvement in rotarod learning, grooming, and reversal learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C122 accurately summarize established literature on striatal function. The citations are appropriate and support the authors' interpretation of their behavioral findings. This provides important context for understanding the significance of the physiological changes.

results.result: Cntnap2-/- mice exhibit enhanced cortical drive of direct pathway striatal projection neurons (dSPNs) due to increased intrinsic excitability rather than changes in synaptic strength. The authors found increased spike probability in dSPNs in response to optogenetic cortical stimulation, but no changes in EPSC amplitude, AMPA:NMDA ratio, or spine density.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirmed these findings. Reviewer 1 stated the study 'describes how deleting...CNTNAP2 in mice increases dorsolateral striatal projection neuron excitability' with 'convincing' evidence. Reviewer 2 noted 'striatal projection neurons (SPNs) are more readily driven to fire action potentials...due to increases in SPN intrinsic excitability rather than changes in excitatory or inhibitory synaptic inputs.' Reviewer 3 confirmed 'increased firing of both types of SPNs in response to cortical afferent stimulation' with 'no significant difference in the amplitude of optically-evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) or spine density.'

results.result: Striatal inhibition mediated by parvalbumin (PV) interneurons is not altered in Cntnap2-/- mice. The authors found no changes in electrically or optically evoked IPSCs, PV interneuron intrinsic excitability, PV cell number, or PV protein expression in the dorsal striatum.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings without challenge. Reviewer 2 noted 'characterization of both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic responses' as a strength. Reviewer 3 stated 'the number and function (IPSC amplitude and intrinsic excitability) of these interneurons in the striatum were comparable to WT controls' and that this finding was 'novel and valuable.' No reviewer questioned the inhibition data.

results.result: Cntnap2-/- dSPNs exhibit significantly increased intrinsic excitability with reduced rheobase current and increased membrane resistance, while iSPNs show only a non-significant trend toward increased excitability. This increased dSPN excitability likely underlies the enhanced corticostriatal drive.
results.evaluation: All reviewers affirmed these findings. Reviewer 1 stated the study 'increases dorsolateral striatal projection neuron excitability' with 'convincing' evidence. Reviewer 2 noted 'increases in SPN intrinsic excitability' as a key finding. Reviewer 3 confirmed 'Cntnap2-/- SPNs, particularly dSPNs, exhibited higher intrinsic excitability, reduced rheobase current and increased membrane resistance' and called this finding 'novel and valuable.'

results.result: The enhanced intrinsic excitability of Cntnap2-/- dSPNs is mediated by altered Kv1.2 channel function, as demonstrated by occlusion of α-DTX effects in knockout dSPNs. The drug α-DTX enhanced firing and decreased threshold in WT but not Cntnap2-/- dSPNs, indicating basal alteration of Kv1.2 channels.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this mechanistic finding. Reviewer 2 stated 'these changes seem to be due to preferential reduction of Kv1.2 in dSPNs.' Reviewer 3 noted the study demonstrates 'increased excitability of striatal projection neurons (SPNs)' and that 'the experiments are well-designed, and the results support the authors' conclusions.' No reviewer challenged the Kv1.2 mechanism.

results.result: Cntnap2-/- mice exhibit increased spontaneous repetitive behaviors including enhanced grooming, marble burying, and nose poking. MoSeq analysis revealed increased grooming syllable frequency, decreased entropy in syllable transitions, and successful genotype decoding based on behavioral patterns.
results.evaluation: All reviewers affirmed these behavioral findings. Reviewer 1 stated the study 'promotes repetitive behaviors' with 'convincing' evidence. Reviewer 2 highlighted 'the use of multiple behavioral techniques, both traditional and cutting-edge machine learning-based analyses' as a strength. Reviewer 3 noted 'Cntnap2-/- mice demonstrated increased repetitive behaviors (RRBs), including more grooming bouts, increased marble burying, and increased nose poking' and called the 'comprehensive behavioral analysis...novel and valuable.'

results.result: Cntnap2-/- mice show increased motor routine learning in the accelerating rotarod task, performing significantly better than WT mice particularly in later trials, with an increased learning rate despite similar initial performance.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding. Reviewer 2 noted the study shows 'enhanced motor learning' as a key result. Reviewer 3 stated the results demonstrate 'altered striatal-dependent behaviors, such as repetitive, inflexible behaviors' and that 'the experiments are well-designed, and the results support the authors' conclusions.' No reviewer questioned the rotarod data.

results.result: Cntnap2-/- mice exhibit cognitive inflexibility and perseveration in a four-choice reversal learning task. While acquisition and recall were normal, knockout mice required significantly more trials during reversal, made more perseverative and regressive errors, and showed decreased latency to make choices, indicating persistence in choosing the previously rewarded odor.
results.evaluation: All reviewers affirmed these findings. Reviewer 1 stated the study demonstrates 'cognitive inflexibility' with 'convincing' evidence. Reviewer 2 noted the authors 'show that CNTNAP2 mice display...cognitive inflexibility.' Reviewer 3 stated 'Cntnap2-/- mice also displayed cognitive inflexibility in a four-choice odor-based reversal learning assay' and that this was 'consistent with potential deficits in corticostriatal function.'

results.result: The authors propose that increased corticostriatal drive may contribute to the acquisition of repetitive, inflexible behaviors in Cntnap2 mice, and speculate that a shared gain-of-function in striatal circuits may play a role in perseverative behaviors across ASD models more broadly.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged this as correlative rather than causal. Reviewer 2 explicitly stated 'the reported changes in dorsolateral striatum SPN excitability are only correlative with reported changes in repetitive behaviors, motor learning and cognitive flexibility' and noted 'the authors do broach this in the text.' Reviewer 3 noted 'it is unclear whether this cellular phenotype alone can account for the behavioral alterations' and that 'the mechanism underlying SPN hyperexcitability was not explored.'

results.result: Cntnap2-/- mice show normal general locomotor activity in the open field but make more entries into the center of the arena, potentially reflecting reduced avoidance behavior.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these findings. The locomotor data served as important controls for the repetitive behavior findings, which all reviewers accepted. No reviewer raised concerns about the open field locomotor measurements.

results.result: Loss of Cntnap2 results in increased excitability of dSPNs likely driven by altered Kv1.2 channel contribution. The authors discuss that loss of Caspr2 has variable impacts on excitability across brain regions and cell types, with increased excitability also observed in cerebellar Purkinje cells and cortical pyramidal cells in some studies.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these summary and discussion points. Reviewer 3 noted 'the results demonstrate that loss of Cntnap2 results in increased excitability of striatal projection neurons (SPNs)' and that 'the experiments are well-designed, and the results support the authors' conclusions.' The discussion of variable effects across brain regions was not challenged.

results.result: The authors discuss inconsistencies in the literature regarding PV interneuron alterations in Cntnap2-/- mice and conclude that primary changes in PV interneurons are unlikely to account for altered striatal circuit function in their model.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this interpretation. Reviewer 3 noted 'despite previous reports of decreased parvalbumin-expressing (PV) interneurons in various brain regions of Cntnap2-/- mice, the number and function...of these interneurons in the striatum were comparable to WT controls' and called this finding 'novel and valuable.' No reviewer challenged the conclusion about PV interneurons.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C49-C55 regarding PV interneuron findings. Both evaluations find the evidence convincing that there are no differences in inhibitory transmission, PV interneuron counts, or PV cell intrinsic excitability. Reviewers explicitly noted this as 'novel and valuable.'

Perfect agreement on claims C75-C76, C81 regarding open field locomotor activity. Both evaluations accept the findings of normal locomotion with increased center entries. These served as important controls for repetitive behavior findings.

Perfect agreement on claims C97-C103 summarizing variable effects across brain regions and cell types. Both evaluations accept the discussion of Kv1.2 channel mechanisms and the synthesis of findings from current and prior literature.
Strong agreement on claims C86-C88 regarding enhanced motor learning on rotarod. Both evaluations accept the dissociation between initial performance and learning rate as well-supported by the data.

Strong agreement on claims C67-C71 regarding α-DTX occlusion experiments and Kv1.2 mechanism. OpenEval notes the occlusion experiment is strong but suggests direct Kv1.2 measurement would strengthen conclusions. Peer reviewers accepted the mechanism without challenge, with Reviewer 2 stating changes 'seem to be due to preferential reduction of Kv1.2 in dSPNs.'

Strong agreement on claims C89-C94, C96 regarding reversal learning deficits. Both evaluations find the behavioral dissociation between normal acquisition and impaired reversal well-characterized, with perseverative and regressive errors driving the deficit.

Strong agreement on claims C77-C80, C82-C83 regarding repetitive behaviors. Both evaluations accept increased grooming, marble burying, and nose poking as well-supported. Peer reviewers highlighted the machine learning-based Keypoint-MoSeq analysis as a particular strength.

Perfect agreement on claims C11, C117, C123-C124 regarding the correlative nature of physiology-behavior links. Both evaluations rate these as UNCERTAIN, noting the lack of causal manipulation experiments. Reviewer 2 explicitly stated findings are 'only correlative' and Reviewer 3 noted 'it is unclear whether this cellular phenotype alone can account for the behavioral alterations.'

Agreement on claims C56-C58, C63 regarding dSPN intrinsic excitability increases. OpenEval addresses C56-C58, C63 while peer review addresses broader set C56-C63. Both find evidence convincing. Peer reviewers called findings 'novel and valuable.'

Agreement on claims C104-C107, C109 regarding inconsistent prior literature on PV interneurons. Both evaluations accept the authors' summary of variable findings across studies and brain regions. Peer reviewers noted the striatal PV findings as 'novel and valuable.'

Partial agreement on synaptic findings. OpenEval R3 addresses claims C42-C45 (no synaptic changes), while peer R1 addresses broader set C5-C6, C39-C45 including both excitability and synaptic findings. Both find the negative synaptic results appropriately rule out synaptic mechanisms.

Partial agreement on increased spike probability in dSPNs. OpenEval R1 addresses claims C39-C40, C5 while peer R1 addresses broader set C5-C6, C39-C45. Both find the increased excitability in response to cortical stimulation well-supported with 'convincing' evidence.

Agreement on speculative nature of broader implications. OpenEval R14 addresses claims C125-C126 as explicitly speculative about generalization to other ASD models. Peer R8 addresses overlapping claims C11, C117, C123-C126 with focus on correlative nature. Both rate as UNCERTAIN, noting appropriate qualification by authors.

Agreement on claims C72-C73 regarding cell-type-specific α-DTX sensitivity. OpenEval R8 focuses on differential sensitivity between dSPNs and iSPNs. Peer R4 addresses broader Kv1.2 mechanism (C67-C73). Both accept the cell-type specificity as well-documented.

Agreement on claims C59-C60 regarding iSPN excitability trends. OpenEval R6 notes appropriate reporting of non-significant trend. Peer R3 addresses broader intrinsic excitability findings (C56-C63) including iSPN data. Both accept the cell-type specificity of the phenotype.

Agreement on claims C61-C62 regarding reduced AP latency in both cell types. OpenEval R17 notes this suggests some shared alterations alongside cell-type-specific effects. Peer R3 addresses broader intrinsic excitability set (C56-C63). Both accept the findings as supported.

Agreement on claims C84-C85 regarding behavioral rigidity measured by Keypoint-MoSeq. OpenEval R10 focuses on reduced entropy and syllable decoding. Peer R5 addresses broader repetitive behavior set (C7, C77-C85) and highlights machine learning analysis as a strength.

Agreement on claim C110 regarding lack of PV interneuron alterations in striatum. OpenEval R19 notes this is reasonable inference from comprehensive negative findings. Peer R11 addresses broader discussion (C104-C110) and calls striatal PV findings 'novel and valuable.'

Agreement on claim C41 regarding non-significant trend in iSPN spike probability. OpenEval R2 commends appropriate statistical interpretation of non-significant result. Peer R1 addresses broader set (C5-C6, C39-C45) but accepts all findings including the iSPN trend data.

OpenEval R20 addresses claims C111-C122 summarizing established literature on striatal function and providing context for behavioral findings. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these background/discussion claims, though peer reviewers accepted the overall behavioral interpretations.
